Socrates challenges this stance using the analogy of the arts to demonstrate that an art works for the benefit of its subjects rather than the practitioner.

entries.label: The Value of Justice Itself
entries.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to prove justice is desirable for its own sake rather than a social compact enforced by the weak. In response, commentary examines the necessity of evaluating justice and moral ideals independently of external rewards or mundane circumstances.

entries.label: The Ideal State and Virtues
entries.summary: Socrates constructs an ideal city to discern justice by analogy with the individual, establishing class structures through the Myth of the Metals and aiming at the well-being of the whole community through education. The commentary examines the prioritization of duty over utility, the distribution of the four cardinal virtues, and civic unity modeled on a single organic body.

entries.label: Nature of the Ideal State
entries.summary: The commentary analyzes the Republic's blend of historical Spartan practices with philosophical idealism, concluding that the city serves as a theoretical pattern rather than an earthly reality. In this light, Plato's detachment from specific Athenian institutions reflects an ideal conception transcending contemporary factional states.

entries.label: Commentary on Plato's Works
entries.summary: These commentary passages evaluate Plato's theoretical proposals, contrasting the hopeful ideal constitution of the Republic with the practical legalism of the Laws, while also rejecting Platonic animal breeding for disregarding the spiritual dignity of human marriage and individuals.

entries.label: Book I: Refuting Thrasymachus
entries.summary: Socrates disputes Thrasymachus by arguing that justice never harms, that rulers err, that arts serve their subjects rather than the practitioner, and that craftsmen do not overreach. He further maintains that injustice undermines cooperation while justice is more profitable, though he concludes Book I in a state of aporia regarding the definition of justice itself.

entries.label: Book II: Glaucon and Adeimantus
entries.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus outline the conventional praise of justice as an external compromise or pursuit of social reward, challenging Socrates to prove the intrinsic value of justice inside the soul apart from any reputational gains.

entries.label: Origins and Analogy of State
entries.summary: Socrates introduces the method of examining justice in the State first before inspecting the individual, and details how the demand for luxury expands the city and leads directly to war.

entries.label: Books III–IV: Civic Order
entries.summary: Socrates establishes criteria for selecting guardian rulers and institutes the Myth of the Metals to fix civic roles, arguing that the city aims at the happiness of the whole rather than a single class and defining justice as each class attending strictly to its proper work.

entries.label: Education and Soul Faculties
entries.summary: Educational reform regulates poetic depictions of divinity and distinguishes internal spiritual falsehood from medicinal state myth. In tandem, physical and musical training balance passion with reason, reflecting the soul's division into rational, spirited, and appetitive elements.

entries.label: Metaphysics and the Good
entries.summary: The realization of the ideal city necessitates philosopher-rulers who differentiate eternal being from opinionated becoming. Their training culminates in the Idea of the Good, illuminated through the sun analogy and the fourfold division of cognition along the Divided Line.

entries.label: Assessments of Platonic Logic
entries.summary: The commentator evaluates Plato's speculative dialectic against modern scientific methods and empirical induction. While praising his ability to disengage abstractions through mathematical study, the critique highlights his tendency to anticipate empirical science without observational facts.

entries.label: The Cave and Higher Studies
entries.summary: The Allegory of the Cave illustrates the soul's conversion from darkness to intelligible light, after which enlightened guardians must return to serve the commonwealth. This ascent is facilitated by mathematics and crowned by dialectic, the supreme study that discards hypotheses to grasp being.

entries.label: Degeneration and Platonic Number
entries.summary: Editorial analysis examines Plato's sequence of constitutional declines as an intellectual and ethical gradation rather than historical chronology, alongside the mathematical and Pythagorean formulation of the human cycle of births.

entries.label: Soul Functions and Moral Order
entries.summary: These entries analyze the functional virtues of the soul, the hierarchical categorization of pleasures according to rational experience, and the merits and fallacies of mapping individual moral faculties directly onto political entities.

entries.label: Aesthetics, Imitation, and Soul
entries.summary: This group explores the pedagogical and spiritual influence of aesthetic forms, contrasting Plato's suspicion of emotional imitation and poetry with arguments for the harmonizing power of music and gymnastics over the soul's spirited and rational faculties.

entries.label: The Good, Ideals, and Rule
entries.summary: Commentary traces the nature of dialectic and the Idea of the Good, evaluating how transcendent ideals, philosopher-statesmen, and spiritual paradigms elevate practical human conduct beyond material necessity.

entries.label: Civic and Inward Justice
entries.summary: Socrates defines civic justice as each person fulfilling their natural occupation and extends this principle inward to establish psychological justice, wherein the tripartite soul achieves temperate harmony under the guidance of reason.

entries.label: Guardianship and State Unity
entries.summary: In Book V dialogue, interlocutors pause Socrates' political overview to demand a full account of the communal family. Socrates responds by prescribing equal education and military duties for female guardians, regulated breeding arrangements, and shared emotional solidarity akin to a single living organism.

entries.label: Aesthetics, Music, and Poetry
entries.summary: These sections assess the cultural and educational roles of art, music, and poetry across Platonic thought. Socrates and the commentator detail the necessity of strict censorship, simple musical modes, and the outright exclusion of imitative poets due to their corrupting influence on the soul.

entries.label: Metaphysics, Soul, and Inquiry
entries.summary: This sequence of editorial analyses outlines Plato's core philosophical framework, spanning the Idea of the Good, theological doctrines of divine truthfulness, and the tripartite psychological structure of the soul. It also traces the educational ascent through dialectic as contrasted with eristic disputation.

entries.label: Justice and Political Order
entries.summary: Commentary entries evaluate Plato's political philosophy, analyzing justice as both internal harmony and functional civic specialization. They review the historical and radical aspects of his communal proposals, the descent through degenerate constitutions, and the composite nature of the ideal state.

entries.label: Critique of Mimetic Poetry
entries.summary: Socrates critiques imitation and poetry as removed from reality, lacking craft knowledge, and inflaming the irrational soul. Consequently, poetical works remain banished from the commonwealth unless defenders establish their moral utility.

entries.label: Soul Divisions and True Pleasure
entries.summary: This sequence explores the tripartite soul, framing inner virtue as psychic health while categorizing desires into necessary and superfluous kinds. Socrates contrasts illusory relief from discomfort with authentic pleasures rooted in enduring truth.

entries.label: Internal Order and Justice
entries.summary: Depicting the soul as a composite of beast, lion, and inner human, Socrates argues that justice consists in rational dominion over base appetites. The individual harmonizes desires according to a transcendent civic model.

entries.label: Knowledge, Opinion, and Kingship
entries.summary: Introducing the paradox of philosopher-kings, Socrates distinguishes seekers of genuine forms from spectators absorbed in sensory particulars. Knowledge and opinion are shown to be completely separate faculties directed toward different realities.

entries.label: Philosophic Rule and Corruption
entries.summary: Philosophers are established as uniquely qualified custodians of civic laws, possessing direct apprehension of eternal reality. However, gifted natures remain vulnerable to environmental corruption, flattery, and popular applause.

entries.label: The Philosopher and the State
entries.summary: These passages address the relationship between philosophic natures and political rule. While current states alienate philosophers, establishing an ideal polity is deemed possible if philosophers rule, and enlightened thinkers must be obliged to leave contemplation to govern the commonwealth.

entries.label: Forms, Good, and Epistemology
entries.summary: This collection examines the intelligible realm, contrasting dialectic with hypothetical arts and mapping the soul's ascent to truth. Key analogies, including the Sun and the Cave, illustrate how pure reason grasps the Idea of the Good and arranges the faculties of the soul.

entries.label: Curriculum for Contemplation
entries.summary: Education is defined as the reorientation of the soul's existing capacity toward true being. A progressive mathematical and philosophical curriculum—spanning arithmetic, geometry, pure astronomy, harmonics, dialectic, and civic duty—systematically draws the mind away from sensory particulars toward the Good.

entries.label: Regimes and Social Decay
entries.summary: Political regimes reflect the character types of their citizens, degenerating through stages of internal division. Oligarchy elevates wealth and fosters a class of disenfranchised drones, which eventually leads to a popular revolution and the establishment of democracy.

entries.label: Dialectical Epistemology
entries.summary: Socrates establishes dialectic and philosophical cognition at the peak of understanding, contrasting mathematical hypothesis and sensible images with unhypothetical first principles and the essential Good.

entries.label: Decline of the State
entries.summary: Socrates outlines the five types of cities and corresponding soul constitutions, tracking the dissolution of the ideal city through civic discord and the subsequent decay from oligarchy into democracy.

entries.label: Rise of Tyranny
entries.summary: Excessive liberty destabilizes the democratic character and state, paving the way for a demagogue to seize power and cultivate lawless, tyrannical appetites.

entries.label: Tyrant's Misery vs True Joy
entries.summary: Socrates evaluates the misery and pervasive fear of public tyrants, proving that the truly just and philosophical life yields the highest pleasure and supreme happiness.

entries.label: Immortality and Soul Rewards
entries.summary: Socrates argues that because the soul cannot be destroyed by internal or external evils, it is immortal, ensuring that virtue receives enduring honors from both gods and humanity.

entries.label: The Myth of Er and Rebirth
entries.summary: Through the visionary Myth of Er, souls choose their next destinies based on philosophical wisdom, leading to the concluding exhortation to pursue righteousness through eternity.

entries.label: Editorial Paratext and Context
entries.summary: Covers Jowett's front matter, dedications, acknowledgments, text revisions, and publishing arrangements for the translation of Plato's works.

entries.label: Dialogue Framing and Structure
entries.summary: Surveys the literary structure of the Republic and Socrates' philosophical trajectory alongside introductory commentaries on early arguments concerning justice.

entries.label: Definitions of Justice in Book I-II
entries.summary: Traces the dramatic dialogue debates over justice, encompassing Cephalus' view of wealth, Polemarchus and Thrasymachus' competing definitions, Socrates' defense of justice as excellence, and Glaucon's challenge via the Ring of Gyges.

entries.label: Ideal State and Guardian Order
entries.summary: Examines the genesis of political order, economic specialization, and the communal structure of the guardian class, including shared property and gender equality.

entries.label: Simplicity in Early Education
entries.summary: Details the principles of simplicity governing early habituation through music, gymnastic training, and physical care, extending these standards to medicine and civic legislation.

entries.label: Philosopher Soul and Education
entries.summary: Explores the soul's internal harmony, the corrupting pressures of public life, advanced dialectical training illustrated by the cave allegory, and lifelong self-education.

entries.label: Tyranny, Cosmology, and Destiny
entries.summary: Contrasts the psychological misery of tyranny with celestial order, moving into the cosmic myth of Er and philosophical reflections on historical progress versus divine faith.

entries.label: Comparative Utopian Politics
entries.summary: Provides critical assessments of Plato's social engineering proposals and traces Platonic political influences across classical, medieval, and Renaissance utopian treatises.

entries.label: Nature and Defense of Justice
entries.summary: Early dialectical encounters examine conventional definitions of justice and Thrasymachus's assertion of might, which Socrates counters via the analogy of the arts and the inherent harmony of virtue. Subsequently, Glaucon and Adeimantus demand an account of justice desired purely for its intrinsic effects within the soul, detached from external rewards or social contracts.

entries.label: The Ideal State and Polity
entries.summary: Socrates establishes the city-state analogy to detect justice on a larger canvas, tracing its expansion from rustic need to luxurious fever and detailing class structures anchored by the Myth of the Metals. Commentators examine these proposals as a theoretical paradigm blending historical Spartan discipline with philosophical ideals, contrasting the Republic's vision with later legalistic frameworks.

entries.label: Education, Art, and the Soul
entries.summary: These texts scrutinize the psychological division of the soul into rational, spirited, and appetitive faculties and outline educational programs to harmonize them. Strict civic and theological censorship regulates poetry and imitation, while commentary both explains Plato's suspicion of theatrical excess and proposes art's potential to convey higher ideal truths.

entries.label: Metaphysics and the Good
entries.summary: The dialogue and editorial assessments present the central metaphysical core of the Republic, including the Allegory of the Cave, the Divided Line, the Sun analogy, and the crowning science of dialectic. Modern commentary weighs Plato's speculative dialectic and mathematical abstraction against empirical induction, evaluating the governing role of transcendent ideals and philosopher-statesmen.

entries.label: Degeneration of Regimes
entries.summary: This sequence examines the downward trajectory of political constitutions and their corresponding soul types through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny. Commentators analyze this progression as an ethical gradation and intellectual model rather than a historical chronology, noting the esoteric role of the Platonic number of births.

entries.label: Civic Order and Soul Training
entries.summary: Socrates describes the formation, discipline, and communal living of the guardian class alongside the rigorous selection required for civic leadership. The discourse regulates music, poetry, medicine, and law to preserve internal harmony, invoking the principle of non-contradiction to ground civic virtues.

entries.label: The Philosopher and the City
entries.summary: Socrates establishes gender equality in civic governance and grounds the ruler's role in the metaphysical distinction between Being and fluctuating opinion. He confronts popular hostility toward philosophers, using the ship parable to defend genuine wisdom against pretenders and proposing gradual public reconciliation.

entries.label: Forms, Curriculum & Dialectic
entries.summary: Through the Cave allegory and structured mathematical sciences, Socrates charts the soul's ascent from shadows to pure contemplation of the Good. The curriculum warns against premature dialectic, examines levels of reality through the Forms, and distinguishes pure pleasures like smell from bodily deficits.

entries.label: Regimes, Tyranny & Cosmic Order
entries.summary: The dialogue outlines the degeneration of constitutions and individual souls from timocracy to despotic tyranny, calculating the extreme misery of the tyrant. It culminates in Er's myth of posthumous cosmic retribution and the harmonious spindle of Necessity.

entries.label: Index and Editorial Apparatus
entries.summary: This paratextual collection indexes references to poetry, the guardian constitution, virtue, and philosopher-rulers, comparing Platonic doctrine with historical Spartan and Athenian models. Editorial notes record textual collation, typographic revisions, and Stephanus numbering conventions.

entries.label: Platonic Philosophy Overview
entries.summary: These editorial commentary sequences review Plato's foundational metaphysics, theology, and psychological faculties alongside his political theories of justice, civic unity, and constitutional degeneration.

entries.label: Civic Unity and Class Order
entries.summary: Socrates details the organization of the ideal state through guardian selection, foundational civic myths, equal duties for female guardians, and communal family structures designed to achieve collective harmony.

entries.label: Psychic Harmony and Desires
entries.summary: This sequence investigates the tripartite soul and psychic health, contrasting necessary appetites with true pleasures and demonstrating that justice entails reason governing the animal and spirited impulses.

entries.label: The Philosopher and Civic Rule
entries.summary: These sections define the nature and virtues of true philosophers, address the paradox of philosopher-kings, and assess both the political obligations of enlightened thinkers and the perils of societal corruption.

entries.label: Intelligible Forms and Dialectic
entries.summary: Socrates contrasts sensory perception and hypothetical reasoning with dialectical ascent, using the Sun, Cave, and Divided Line analogies to demonstrate how intelligence grasps unhypothetical reality and the supreme Good.

entries.label: Degeneration and Tyranny
entries.summary: This sequence charts the progressive decline of cities and soul types from aristocracy to tyranny, contrasting the lawless misery and fear of the public tyrant with the superior happiness of the philosophical life.

entries.label: Critique of Mimetic Art and Poetry
entries.summary: Socrates and paratextual commentaries critique imitative poetry and music as distant from reality and harmful to the irrational soul, mandating strict cultural censorship and the exclusion of poetical works from the commonwealth.

entries.label: Soul Purity, Rebirth, and Er
entries.summary: These passages argue for the soul's imperishable nature when viewed in pristine purity, vindicate the enduring rewards of virtue, and culminate in the Myth of Er where souls choose their cyclical destinies through wisdom.

entries.label: Editorial and Dialogue Intro
entries.summary: Surveys the introductory apparatus of the Republic, bringing together editorial framing, publication details, and contextual overviews of Plato's dramatic structure. It also presents the initial character encounters that set up the broader inquiry into justice.

entries.label: Early Debates on Justice
entries.summary: Details the dramatic challenges and arguments regarding justice presented in Books I and II. These cover conventional views, Thrasymachus's cynical definitions of power, and Glaucon and Adeimantus's demand to prove justice desirable entirely for its own sake.

entries.label: The Ideal State and Polity
entries.summary: Explores the structural founding of the ideal city, tracing the progression from primitive association to specialized classes and guardian disciplines. It synthesizes discussions on social organization, property, and class roles with comparative and later utopian political thought.

entries.label: Education, Arts, and the Soul
entries.summary: Examines early educational conditioning in music, poetry, and bodily discipline alongside the psychological division of the soul. The selections assess the moral influence of cultural censorship and the cultivation of temperance and psychic harmony.

entries.label: Dialectic and Philosopher Rulers
entries.summary: Analyzes the philosophical apex of the dialogue, including the metaphysical allegories of the Cave, Sun, and Divided Line, alongside the advanced dialectical curriculum. It addresses the character, education, and civic obligations of the philosopher-king.

entries.label: Regime Decline and Destiny
entries.summary: Follows the ethical and political degeneration of constitutions from timocracy down to tyranny, illustrating the corresponding misery of the tyrannical soul. The sequence concludes with cosmological reflections, the Myth of Er, and broader patterns of destiny and divine order.

entries.label: Civic Order and Guardianship
entries.summary: These discussions define the institutional foundation of the ideal commonwealth through the strict selection, education, and communal living of the guardian class. They outline civic myths, division of functions, equal duties for women, and the psychological and legal disciplines required to maintain communal unity.

entries.label: The Philosopher and Civic Rule
entries.summary: This sequence addresses the paradox of philosopher-kings and the metaphysical distinction between eternal Being and shifting opinion. It confronts popular hostility and the perils of societal corruption, defending true philosophical rule and exploring the obligations of enlightened thinkers within the city.

entries.label: Dialectic, Forms, and the Soul
entries.summary: These passages trace the soul's ascent from sensory illusions and bodily desires to the contemplation of unhypothetical reality and the supreme Good. Utilizing the allegories of the Sun, Cave, and Divided Line alongside higher mathematical curricula, they ground psychic harmony in the rule of reason over appetitive impulses.

entries.label: Regimes, Degeneration, and Er
entries.summary: The dialogue charts the progressive moral and political decline from aristocracy to despotic tyranny, demonstrating the misery of the tyrannical soul in contrast to the just life. It concludes with the demonstration of the soul's immortality and the Myth of Er, which depicts cosmic judgment, the spindle of Necessity, and the cyclical choice of destiny.

entries.label: Critique and Paratextual Index
entries.summary: This group encompasses comprehensive editorial overviews, detailed subject indices, and textual notes alongside the critique of mimetic art and poetry. It surveys Platonic metaphysics, psychology, and civic models while recording editorial collation and conventions.

entries.label: Dialogue Framing and Justice
entries.summary: This sequence combines the introductory apparatus, historical context, and dramatic opening encounters with the foundational debates of Books I and II. It follows the inquiry from conventional maxims of justice through Thrasymachus's radical challenge and the demand by Glaucon and Adeimantus to defend justice as an intrinsic good.

entries.label: The Ideal City and Guardians
entries.summary: These passages detail the theoretical origin, structural hierarchy, and practical institutions of the ideal commonwealth. They address division of labour, guardian selection and discipline, communal property, the inclusion and role of women, and the civic unity needed to maintain an organic political body.

entries.label: Psychology, Culture, and Arts
entries.summary: This division unites discussions on early cultural education, the regulation of poetry and musical modes, and the tripartite psychological nature of the soul with retrospective critiques of mimetic art and comprehensive indices. It contrasts harmonic cultural formation with the severe philosophical censure of imitation.

entries.label: Metaphysics and Philosopher-Kings
entries.summary: Focusing on the philosophical center of the Republic, this group examines the rule of philosopher-kings, the distinction between true knowledge and mere opinion, and the metaphysical allegories of the Sun, Divided Line, and Cave. It explores the higher dialectical curriculum, the contemplation of the Idea of the Good, and the political necessity and difficulty of descending back into civic governance.

entries.label: Regime Decline and Destiny
entries.summary: Tracing the ethical and political degeneration of constitutions from aristocracy down through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny, these clusters contrast the disordered tyrannical soul with the happiness of the just life. They conclude with cosmological investigations, the demonstration of the immortality of the soul, and the Myth of Er's vision of cosmic necessity and moral choice.
